narr: Let's explore the history of Uzbekistan, focusing on weeks five and six of our course.
We'll start by examining key terms related to labor and important historical dates.

data.heading: Forced/Compulsory Labor
bullets: All work or service which is exacted from any person under the menace of any penalty and for which the said person has not offered himself voluntarily (ILO Convention No. 29, Art. 2)

narr: First, let's understand the concept of forced or compulsory labor.
According to ILO Convention No. 29, it's any work extracted from a person under penalty threat that they haven't voluntarily undertaken.

data.heading: Key ILO Conventions
bullets: Convention No. 29 (1930): ILO's fundamental convention on forced labor: definition and list of exceptions
Convention No. 105 (1957): prohibits forced labor in five cases: political, economic development, discipline, strikes, discrimination
2014 Protocol: supplements Convention No. 29 with national policy and action plans; ratified by Uzbekistan on June 25, 2019
Convention No. 182 (1999): on the worst forms of child labor; ratified by Uzbekistan in March 2008
Convention No. 138 (1973): on minimum age for employment; ratified in March 2009
ILO: International Labour Organization; Uzbekistan has ratified 17 conventions (8 fundamental) and 1 protocol

narr: Several important ILO conventions relate to forced labor.
Convention No. 29 from 1930 provides the fundamental definition and exceptions.
Convention No. 105 from 1957 specifically prohibits forced labor in five cases: political coercion, economic development, disciplinary measures, during strikes, and for discrimination.
In 2014, a protocol was added to supplement Convention No. 29 with national policy requirements, which Uzbekistan ratified in 2019.
Convention No. 182 addresses the worst forms of child labor, ratified by Uzbekistan in 2008.
Convention No. 138 sets minimum age for employment, ratified in 2009.
The International Labour Organization itself has seen Uzbekistan ratify 17 conventions, including 8 fundamental ones, plus one protocol.

data.heading: Uzbek Terms and Institutions
bullets: Majburiy mehnat: Uzbek term used as a single concept of forced and compulsory labor
Hashar: "voluntary, selfless participation of the majority in completing a task"; conditions — resolution of the CM No. 349 of May 10, 2018
National Commission: commission on combating human trafficking and forced labor; established by decree PF-5775 of July 30, 2019
National Rapporteur: an institution that reports annually to the President on the situation with forced labor
Labour Inspection: an agency that identifies violations of labor rights; under resolution No. 1066 of December 31, 2018, has the right to transfer materials to court
Third-party monitoring: monitoring of child and forced labor by ILO experts and human rights defenders (since 2013)

narr: Let's examine some Uzbek terminology and institutions related to labor issues.
Majburiy mehnat is the Uzbek term encompassing forced and compulsory labor.
Hashar refers to 'voluntary, selfless participation,' though its conditions were formalized in a 2018 resolution.
The National Commission was established in 2019 specifically to combat human trafficking and forced labor.
The National Rapporteur institution reports annually to the President on forced labor situations.
The Labour Inspection agency identifies labor rights violations and gained court transfer rights in 2018.
Third-party monitoring by ILO experts and human rights defenders has been in place since 2013.

data.heading: Cotton Labor Issues
bullets: Cotton monoculture: an economic structure inherited from the empire and the USSR; according to Bhat — the primary cause of forced child labor
Child labour: mass mobilization of schoolchildren for cotton harvesting; systematic use eliminated by 2019

narr: Cotton production has been central to Uzbekistan's labor issues.
The monoculture economy, inherited from previous regimes, is identified by Bhat as the primary cause of forced child labor.
Historically, there was mass mobilization of schoolchildren for cotton harvesting, though this systematic practice was reportedly eliminated by 2019.
Now, let's review the key dates and numbers from weeks five and six that you'll need for your exam.
These dates cover important events in Uzbekistan's legal and labor history.

events.text: Cotton plantations in Turkestan increased from 41,000 to 92,888 dessiatines (Bhat)
The Emperor approved the "Regulation on the Administration of the Turkestan Region" — the main legal document of the region (Yusupjanova)
Third stage of judicial reforms: a judicial chamber was created — the highest authority in Turkestan (Yusupjanova)
Fourth stage of reforms: adaptation of the judicial system to the Judicial Statutes of the Russian Empire (Yusupjanova)

narr: Let's begin with the late 19th and early 20th century.
Between 1886 and 1900, cotton plantations in Turkestan significantly expanded from 41,000 to 92,888 dessiatines.
On June 12, 1886, the Emperor approved the "Regulation on the Administration of the Turkestan Region," which became the main legal document for the region.
During 1897-1899, the third stage of judicial reforms established a judicial chamber as the highest authority in Turkestan.
Then from 1898 to 1917, the fourth stage adapted the judicial system to the Russian Empire's Judicial Statutes.

events.text: Introduction of the first systematic Criminal Procedure Code — completion of the first stage of judicial policy in Turkestan (Yusupjanova)
Law "On the Judicial System of the USSR, Union and Autonomous Republics": 8 chapters, 80 articles (Komolov)
German invasion; provisions "On the State of War" and "On Military Tribunals" were adopted (Komolov)
Decrees of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR on labor days for collective farm workers and mobilization of city dwellers for agricultural work (Komolov)
Congress of Judges of the Republic: combating theft, the role of courts in the 1944 cotton harvest (Komolov)

narr: Moving to the Soviet era, on August 1, 1922, the first systematic Criminal Procedure Code was introduced, completing the first stage of judicial policy in Turkestan.
On August 16, 1938, the Law "On the Judicial System of the USSR" was established with 8 chapters and 80 articles.
With the German invasion on June 22, 1941, provisions "On the State of War" and "On Military Tribunals" were adopted.
On April 13, 1942, decrees established labor days for collective farm workers and mobilized city dwellers for agricultural work.
On September 10, 1944, a Congress of Judges addressed combating theft and the role of courts in the 1944 cotton harvest.

events.text: Approval of the Criminal Procedure Code of the Uzbek SSR / its introduction into legal practice (Yusupjanova)
Declaration of independence; decision to create a Constitutional Commission of 64 people (Buronov; Azizov)
Meeting of the Constitutional Commission: beginning of direct work on the draft (Buronov)
Constitutional Law "On the Foundations of State Independence" (17 articles) (Buronov; Azizov)
First draft of the Constitution: 158 articles, six sections (Buronov)

narr: In the post-Soviet period, on May 21, 1959, the Criminal Procedure Code of the Uzbek SSR was approved, taking effect January 1, 1960.
On June 20, 1990, Uzbekistan declared independence and decided to create a 64-member Constitutional Commission.
On April 12, 1991, the Constitutional Commission began direct work on the constitutional draft.
On August 31, 1991, the Constitutional Law "On the Foundations of State Independence" with 17 articles was adopted.
Between October and November 1991, the first draft of the Constitution was created with 158 articles across six sections.

events.text: Partial renewal of the composition of the Constitutional Commission — up to 71 members (Buronov)
Publication of the draft Constitution for nationwide discussion (Buronov)
Second publication of the draft: discussion in two stages (Buronov)
Last meeting of the commission; the eleventh session of the Supreme Council adopted the Constitution (Buronov)
Adoption of 15 codes — establishment of legal branches (Azizov)

narr: Continuing with constitutional development, on July 2-3, 1992, the Constitutional Commission was partially renewed with up to 71 members.
On September 26, 1992, the draft Constitution was published for nationwide discussion.
On November 21, 1992, a second publication of the draft initiated a two-stage discussion process.
On December 7-8, 1992, the commission held its last meeting, and the Supreme Council adopted the Constitution during its eleventh session.
From 1994 to 2008, 15 codes were adopted, establishing various legal branches.

events.text: Abolition of the death penalty and transfer of arrest sanctions to courts (Azizov); Law "On Guarantees of the Child's Right to Work" (Bhat)
Ratification of ILO Conventions No. 182 and No. 138 (Bhat)
Resolution of the CM No. 349 "On Additional Measures to Eliminate Forced Labor" (Sulaimanov, Rasulov)

narr: In more recent developments, 2007 saw the abolition of the death penalty and transfer of arrest sanctions to courts, plus the Law "On Guarantees of the Child's Right to Work."
In March 2008 and 2009, Uzbekistan ratified ILO Conventions No. 182 and No. 138 respectively.
On May 10, 2018, Resolution No. 349 was passed on additional measures to eliminate forced labor.
